segments.heading: Function `short_version`: the text of section 0
segments.text:
These lines are inside the function `render`, which starts at line 341.
- `short_version` is defined inside `render`. It can read the variables of `render`.
- It does not run at this place. `render` calls it at line 1467 with the dictionary `ctx` as `c`. By then `section4` of facts_text4.py has added its results to `ctx`.
- It computes no rate. It takes lowest and highest values, differences and counts from record lists that already hold `GBps`, and it rounds them for the text.

These two lines take six results of `section4` out of `c` [Ref3]:
- `by` (`c['byst']`): the oldread and asmread ranges of the 8000 MT/s pool L-1 to L-4, split by the start state of the process.
- `pcv` (`c['partC_view']`): oldread of part C compared with the pool processes that started after 120-thread work.
- `kF1`, `kI1`: asmread of F72d12 and of control I, each compared with the data set L-1 alone.
- `kAao`: the part C asmread intervals that ran directly after oldread, compared with the asmread pool of L-1 to L-4.
- `oth` (`c['byst_other']`): oldread ranges of the runners bwx11 and bwx for processes that started after 120-thread work.

A comparison such as `kAao` is a result of `compare` (line 333). Its key `a` is the 7200 MT/s range, `b` is the 8000 MT/s range, and `dist` is the distance of the nearest ends in GB/s. This guard needs no overlap and a distance above 0. Then every part C asmread interval that ran directly after oldread is above the highest asmread rate of the 8000 MT/s pool.

`A72o` holds the `bw_old read` intervals of part A from all sessions and rounds (line 419). `cAo['b']` is the range of `bw_old read` in the 8000 MT/s data sets A-1 to A-3 (line 425).
- `a_lo` counts the intervals of `A72o` whose `GBps` is below the lowest 8000 MT/s rate.
- `a_hi` counts the intervals whose `GBps` is above the highest 8000 MT/s rate.
- Both tests are strict (`<`, `>`), and they use the values before rounding.
- The guard needs at least one interval on each side. It also needs the 7200 MT/s range (`hi - lo`, in GB/s) to be wider than the 8000 MT/s range.

- Line 485: guard. The asmread range of F72d12 must lie inside the asmread range of the 8000 MT/s pool (`inside`, line 468).
- `nL`: the text for n of the oldread intervals of part L. `nns` writes it as intervals / processes / sessions / boots.
- `nP`: the text for n of the 8000 MT/s oldread pool. `nn` writes it as intervals / processes / boots.
- Line 487: guard. The asmread side must give the same two texts. So the sentences below use `nL` and `nP` for both kernels.

`short` is the list of the three sentences. Sentence 1 answers Q1 from the read intervals of part C.
- `c_ro[1]`: the drops of the group "read after oldread". `c_ra[1]`: the drops of the group "read after asmread" (lines 402 to 409 and 470).
- One drop is `(1 - GBps of read / GBps of oldread) x 100`, in percent. Both intervals come from the same process and round (lines 309 to 314).
- In the group "read after asmread" (the crev processes) the oldread interval of the pair is the last of its round. It ran after the read interval.
- `pcr` takes the lowest and the highest drop of a list and prints each with 1 decimal, half up.
- `secX` is the interval length of the bwx12 parts as text. `len(c_ro[1])` is the number of pairs per group. The guard of line 471 checks that both groups hold the same number.
- The word "yes" is fixed text. The guard of line 396 checks it: every drop must be above 0.

Sentence 2 is about the old read kernel in Q2.
- `SAME` is the fixed wording. The guard of line 464 checks that part A (`cAo`) and part C (`cCo`) overlap their 8000 MT/s ranges.
- `pc(cAo['width'])`, `pc(cCo['width'])`: the width of each 8000 MT/s range, `(hi - lo) / lo x 100`, in percent with 1 decimal.
- `sp(cLo['a'])`: the lowest and the highest oldread rate of part L. `sp(cLo['b'])`: the lowest and the highest rate of the 8000 MT/s oldread pool (L-1 to L-4, position 0). `sp` prints each end with 2 decimals.
- The words "the rate was lower in part L" are fixed text. The guard of line 465 checks them.

Sentence 3 is about the load-only loop in Q2. It uses asmread in place of the new read kernel.
- `sp(cLa['a'])` against `sp(cLa['b'])`: the asmread range of part L against the asmread range of the 8000 MT/s pool (L-1 to L-4, position 1).
- `sp(cIa['a'])`, `nns(I72a)`: the asmread range of control I and its n.
- `kAao['a']['n']`, `sp(kAao['a'])`: the number and the range of the part C asmread intervals that ran directly after oldread.
- `sp(cFa['a'])`, `nns(F72a)`: the asmread range of F72d12 and its n.
- The words "ran above every bwx12 row" are fixed text. Guards check them: line 462 for part L, line 480 for part C, and a guard in `section4` for control I [Ref3].

`detail` is the list of the 12 detail lines. The first two are about Q1.
- `dl`: the drops of part L (line 390). Each one compares the asmread interval with the oldread interval of the same process and round.
- `dpa`: the drops of part A (line 395). Each one compares the median of the 3 `bw_new read` intervals with the median of the 3 `bw_old read` intervals of the same session and round.
- `pcr` prints the lowest and the highest drop of each list. `len` gives the number of pairs. In this run each list holds 6 drops [Ref4].
- `secA` is the interval length of part A as text.

Detail line 3 gives the numbers behind the wording `SAME` of sentence 2.
- Part A: `sp(cAo['a'])` is the lowest and the highest rate of all `bw_old read` intervals of part A. `sp(cAo['b'])` is the same for the data sets A-1 to A-3.
- Part C: `sp(cCo['a'])` covers all oldread intervals of part C. `sp(cCo['b'])` covers the 8000 MT/s oldread pool.
- `pc(cAo['width'])`, `pc(cCo['width'])`: the widths of the two 8000 MT/s ranges in percent of their lower ends.
- `g(cAo['a']['hi'] - cAo['a']['lo'])`: the width of the 7200 MT/s range of part A in GB/s. The difference is taken before rounding. The next value is the same for the 8000 MT/s range.
- `a_lo`, `a_hi`: the counts of lines 481 and 482. `cAo['a']['n']`: the number of `bw_old read` intervals of part A.

- Lines 519 to 521: detail line 4 is fixed text about the rules for part C.
- Lines 522 to 525: detail line 5 gives the oldread ranges of F72d12 (`cFo['a']`) and of control I (`cIo['a']`), each with its number of processes.
- `hm(f72t)[:5]` is the launch time of the F72d12 process as hours and minutes (line 379).
- The words "lie inside the range" are fixed text. The guard of line 469 checks them.

Detail line 6 quotes the view by start state that `section4` computed [Ref3].
- `by['Bo']`: the oldread range (position 0) of the pool processes that were launched at a 1-minute load average of 1.0 or more. A guard in `section4` checks that each of them started at most 30 s after the end of a 120-thread bwx12 process.
- `by['gaps'][0]`, `by['gaps'][-1]`: the shortest and the longest time between the end of that 120-thread process and the launch, printed in whole seconds.
- `by['near']`: the lowest rate of `by['Bo']` minus the highest oldread rate of part L, in GB/s. `pcv['near']`: the same for part C.
- `oth['b11']`, `oth['bx0']`: the oldread ranges (position 0) of bwx11 and of the first runner bwx. `nn(..., boots=False)` writes n as intervals / processes.
- Line 535: detail line 7 is fixed text plus the constant `H1_MEAS` (line 26).

Detail line 8 is about asmread in the three visits of the 7200 MT/s boot.
- `kF1['dist']`: the lowest asmread rate of F72d12 minus the highest asmread rate of L-1 alone, in GB/s.
- `c['f72_limit']`: a sentence that `section4` built about the process list of F72d12 [Ref3].
- `cIa['dist']`: the lowest asmread rate of control I minus the highest rate of the pool L-1 to L-4. `kI1['dist']`: the same against L-1 alone.
- `rng(F72a + L72a + I72a)`: the three record lists are joined to one list. `rng` takes the lowest and the highest `GBps` of all asmread intervals of F72d12, part L and control I. No rates are added.

- Lines 543 to 548: detail line 9 prints the comparison `kAao`. The values are the range and n of the part C asmread intervals directly after oldread (`c['Aao']`), the wording, the range and n of the 8000 MT/s asmread pool, and the distance of the nearest ends.
- The guard of line 480 allows no overlap. So `kAao['wording']` is `DIFFERS` here.
- Lines 549 and 550: detail line 10 is fixed text. The guard of line 467 checks its first sentence: in session 1 of part A every `bw_new read` interval is above the 8000 MT/s range of its round.

- Lines 551 to 555: detail line 11. `c['hw']['low_a']['GBps']` is the lowest asmread rate of the 8000 MT/s pool. `c['hw']['wo']` is the range of the pool without that one interval. `section4` computes both [Ref3].
- The count "2 corrected records" and the words "no wording changes" are fixed text. Guards in `section4` check them [Ref3].
- Lines 556 and 557: detail line 12 is fixed text.

Line 559 stores the three sentences and the 12 detail lines in the verdict object `V`. So facts.json holds them too. Lines 560 to 563 build the lines for the sheet: each sentence with an empty line after it, the line "More detail for these three sentences:", and one bullet per detail line. `render` inserts the returned list at the index `i_short` (line 1467).

segments.heading: Section 0: the word list
segments.text:
After the definition of `short_version`, `render` continues here.
- These lines write the first lines of a folded block (`<details>`). A browser shows it closed until the reader opens it.
- `words` is a list of 52 pairs: a term and its definition.
- 41 definitions are fixed text. 11 definitions get a value or a reference number, as the next rows say.

Definitions of the machine, the kernels, the binaries and the parts of the run. All are fixed text. Only line 572 inserts a value: `mib`, the buffer size per thread. It comes from the P rows of the bwx12 files of the rerun (lines 376 and 377).
The entry for control I gets the two constants `ADDED` and `NOT_PLAN` (lines 24 and 25). The other entries of these lines are fixed text.

Entries on the row kinds of a bwx csv file (lines 605 to 607) and on how a rate is measured. They are fixed text with two values from the records.
- "Whole-pass stop" and "Common stop" (lines 608 to 610) say what ends a timed interval in part A and in the bwx12 parts.
- `secA`, `secX`: the interval lengths of part A and of the bwx12 parts, from the field `min_ms` of the records (lines 372 to 374).
- "Pass count" (lines 611 to 615) says that copy and asmcopy count read plus written bytes.
- "Rate, total" (lines 616 and 617) names the two sources of a rate. Part A: the column `aggregate_GBps` that the benchmark prints. bwx runners: the bytes of each thread are divided by the elapsed time of that thread and by 1e9, and the values of all threads are added [Ref2].
- The entry does not give the formula of `aggregate_GBps`. The header line of each process in `threads120.csv` gives it: the sum of the bytes divided by the longest elapsed time of a thread [Ref7].

Entries about the machine state. Each `ref(...)` call inserts the reference number of a source: the manual pages for the load average and for `%CPU`, the DIMM report, and the saved module list. Line 633 inserts the number of "Memory Device" entries that `build_facts.py` counted in the module list [Ref1]. The other words are fixed text.
The remaining entries are fixed text: 2 MiB pages, marker file, governor, rc, sha256, and the terms of the comparison rules (baseline, ranges overlap, n, pool, distance of the nearest ends).

Guard for the definitions that quote the DIMM report.
- `fd._open` opens the report and adds its path to the list `OPENED` of facts_data.py. A guard near the end of `render` (line 1475) stops the script when an opened file is not in the file list of section 7.
- The guard of these lines checks that six fixed texts are in the report, character by character. If one is missing, the script stops.
Writes one bullet line per entry, with the term in bold. Then it closes the block.
Writes the request of the user as a quote, and the two questions Q1 and Q2. All of it is fixed text.

segments.heading: Section 1.1: steps and times
segments.text:
Writes the headings of section 1 and of section 1.1, and three bullets.
- `go_start`, `go_end`: the times of the first and the last state line of the go.sh log (line 371). `go2_start`, `go2_end`: the same for the go2.sh log (line 378).
- `hm` prints a time as `HH:MM:SS`. Each `ref(...)` call adds the reference number of a log or of go.sh.
- The third bullet (lines 695 and 696) is fixed text about the order of the sessions.

Builds one table row per step and adds the table with `table` (line 132). `ev` holds the steps in the order of their first launch [Ref1]. `o` is the folder record of the step.
- Part A step: the text names the session and the count of 24 processes, which is fixed text. The sources are `threads120.csv` and probe.txt. `last` is the launch time of the last process.
- bwx12 step: the text is part L, part C with the name of its spec file, or control I. A session number is added only for a part L or part C step that has one. The source is launches.txt. `last` is `-`.
- Line 711: `e['start']` is the time in the folder name. `e['first']` is the first launch. `e['end']` is the end of the last process.
- Line 712: the gap in whole seconds, or `-` when the step has none.

Writes five notes under the table.
- Lines 715 to 718: three notes of fixed text. They say where the columns "Script start", "End of last process" and "Gap" come from.
- Lines 719 and 720: a note on the 1 s resolution of the time stamps, with the reference number of rx.sh.
- Lines 721 and 722: T72A1 has no gap. The note prints the three load averages of the first state line of the go.sh log, each with 2 decimals.

segments.heading: Section 1.2: machine state and its proof
segments.text: Writes the heading and one line of introduction. The list `rows` of line 730 is not used in this section. Line 854 gives the name a new list.

`procs_str` turns the process counts per user of one state line into text. `p` maps a user name to a number of processes. The text gives the count of `jhan`, the count of `root`, the number of other accounts and the sum of their processes.

Reads the text of ra.sh (the script of part A) and takes two numbers out of it with regular expressions.
- `ra_limit`: the number after `$r -le`. The wait loop of ra.sh ends when the count of runnable tasks is at or below it.
- `ra_sleep`: the number in the first line that starts with `sleep`. ra.sh waits this number of seconds after the loop.
- The lines below use `ra_sleep`. Section 1.5 uses `ra_limit` (line 950).

Collects the state lines of the two logs. `go` and `go2` hold the parsed logs of go.sh and go2.sh. Each entry of `statelist` is a pair: the time of the line, and its table row. The row holds the log name with line number and label, the time, the first 8 characters of the boot id, MemTotal, the three load averages, runnable tasks / all tasks, the logins, the state of the marker file, and the text of `procs_str`.

Adds two rows per part A folder from its probe.txt.
- Start row: time, boot id, MemTotal, load averages and logins of the first probe lines. The runnable count gets the note that it was read at least `ra_sleep` seconds before this time.
- End row: time, MemTotal and load averages of the `load_after` line.
- A value that probe.txt does not hold is written as `not recorded`.
Sorts all rows by their time and adds the table. The sort of Python keeps the order of insertion for rows with the same time. So a log row stands before a probe.txt row of the same second.

- `sysacc`: the user names other than `jhan` and `root` that own processes in a state line. `users`: all user names. `nst`: the number of state lines of both logs.
- Lines 761 and 762 write the bullet on the boot id. The full boot id comes from try6.txt.
- Lines 763 to 765 write the bullet on the 12 modules: MemTotal, its line number in try6.txt, the number in the kernel message and its line number.
- The words "all" and "in every line" are fixed text. The integrity checks `boot` and `memtotal` of `build_facts.py` test them [Ref1]. A guard in `section4` stops the script when a check failed [Ref3].

Loads the data for the proof of the module count and runs six guards. `md` holds values that `build_facts.py` read from the saved journal h-1.txt, two kernel logs, the module list and try6.txt [Ref1].
- Line 769: the boot table of the DIMM report lists exactly one boot with the start minute of the journal h-1.txt. Both sources give 10 modules for it. The journal h-5.txt gives 12.
- Lines 771 to 775: four fixed texts stand in the DIMM report.
- Lines 776 to 778: the "Memory:" line of each kernel log carries the start time of the journal of the same boot (h-1.txt or h-5.txt).
- Line 779: the two totals differ by exactly 64 x 1024 x 1024 K.
- Lines 781 to 783: the module list holds 12 entries, 12 speed lines and 12 lines of each of the two size kinds. The speed line of try6.txt gives 12 too. The count of all size lines equals the value `modules=` of try6.txt.
- Line 784: the file time of the module list lies inside the time span of row 0 of boots.txt.

Writes two bullets.
- Lines 785 to 789: why the kernel message proves the module count. The values are the start of the 10-module boot (`hmd` prints date and time), its module count, the line number in the journal, and the count from the boot table.
- Lines 790 to 796: the direct count. The values are the speed line of try6.txt, the file time of the module list, and the counts of its "Memory Device" entries and of its speed lines.

- Lines 797 to 804: the bullet on the memory size. `g(try6['memtotal_kB'] / 1024 / 1024)` converts MemTotal from kB to GiB and prints 2 decimals. The other values are the two numbers and the line number of each "Memory:" line, and the difference of the two totals.
- The date 2026-11-09 and the value 384 GiB in this bullet are fixed text.
- Lines 805 to 809: the bullet on the line `modules=` of try6.txt. It prints the three counts of the size lines of the module list. The hypothesis in it is fixed text.

Three bullets.
- Lines 810 to 814: the memory speed. Line number, count and speed come from the speed line of try6.txt. `hm(try6['utc'])` is the time in the first line of try6.txt. The assumption that the speed does not change inside one boot is fixed text.
- Lines 815 and 816: the time since boot. It is the start of go.sh minus the time of the first kernel log line of this boot. `dur` prints it as hours, minutes and seconds.
- Lines 817 and 818: the Linux kernel command line and its line number in the go.sh log.

- `gv` is the governors line of the go.sh log. `gov` holds every pair of a CPU count and a governor name in it. `cur` is the number after `scaling_cur_freq`.
- The guard of line 822 checks that the line names one governor only.
- Lines 823 to 825 print the count, the governor and `cur`. `cur / 1e6` converts kHz to GHz, printed with 1 decimal.
- Lines 826 to 828 split the huge page line of the log into the values of `enabled` and `defrag` and print both.

The remaining bullets of section 1.2.
- Lines 829 to 832: the runnable count of probe.txt. The values are `ra_sleep` and the distinct counts of the probe.txt files.
- Line 833 is fixed text about the logins. Line 840 says that the marker file is absent in all `nst` state lines. The integrity check `logins` of `build_facts.py` tests both statements [Ref1].
- Lines 834 to 839: the users that own processes. `jh` holds the distinct counts of `jhan`. `rt` holds the count of `root` per state line, and the text prints its lowest and its highest value.
- The words "own 1 each" of line 838 are fixed text. No `need` call and no integrity check tests them.
- Lines 841 to 844: the CPU affinity line of the go.sh log, and the value `hwerr=` of try6.txt with its time.

segments.heading: Section 1.3: system load at every launch
segments.text: Writes the heading and two lines of fixed text. The first says where the load value comes from: the run script reads the 1-minute load average directly before it starts a process. The second says that ra.sh writes the value into the "-- binary" line of each process.

The table of part A: one row per session. `ls` holds the load at launch of each process of the session, from its header line in `threads120.csv`. The row gives the three load averages of probe.txt before the first process, the runnable count, the load at the first launch, the lowest and the highest load of all launches, the number of launches, the three load averages after the last process, and the highest `%CPU` of the process list in probe.txt.

The table of the bwx12 steps: one row per folder of parts L and C and of control I, in the order of the launch time. `la` is the launch line of launches.txt. The row gives the launch time, the three load averages, runnable tasks / all tasks, the logins, and the highest `%CPU` of the process list in env.txt.

Notes on the load, with their guards.
- `hi`, `lo`: the bwx12 steps with a load at launch of 1.0 or more, and below 1.0. The guard of line 877 checks that `lo` holds exactly the two control I steps.
- `s1l`: the loads of the launches of session 1 of part A, in file order. The guard of line 880 checks that the load never falls from one launch to the next.
- `rest`: the loads of all launches of sessions 2 and 3 of part A and of the steps in `hi`. Lines 883 and 884 print the lowest and the highest. Line 885 prints the loads of the steps in `lo`.
- The guard of line 886 checks that exactly 1 task was runnable at every bwx12 launch.

- `envgap`: for each bwx12 step, the launch time minus the time in the first line of env.txt, in seconds. The guard checks that every value is above 0. So env.txt was written before the launch.
- Lines 890 to 895 print the highest `%CPU` of all env.txt files, the smallest and the largest of these differences, and the number of launches. The rest is fixed text about the limit of `%CPU`.
- Lines 896 and 897: fixed text about the process lists of probe.txt, with the reference number of ra.sh.

The hypothesis on the high load values.
- `ev_near`: the steps that have a gap and are not control I. `ev_far`: the control I steps.
- The guard of lines 900 to 902 checks four things. The first step is T72A1 and has no gap. The two lists hold all other steps. Every gap in `ev_near` is below 10 s. Every gap in `ev_far` is above 10 s.
- Lines 903 to 914 write the bullet. The values are the number of steps in `ev_near`, their first and last tag, their distinct gaps, the load of the first step, and the tags, gaps and loads of the control I steps.
- The hypothesis and the check that would test it are fixed text.

segments.heading: Section 1.4: integrity checks
segments.text:
Writes one numbered line per integrity check of `D['checks']`: the number, `pass` or `FAILED`, and the text of the check.
- `build_facts.py` ran the checks before it called `render` [Ref1].
- Three checks test the rates. One compares the rate from the T rows (the sum of the thread rates) with `aggregate_GBps` of the I row of the same interval. Its pass limit is a difference below 0.05 GB/s. It covers only the 9 bwx12 files of the rerun. Two compare the intervals with the output of stat_k120.py and stat_bwx.py (two earlier analysis scripts in `S`).
- A guard in `section4` stops the script when a check failed [Ref3]. So a sheet that was written shows `pass` in every line.

Writes the bullet on 2 MiB pages.
- `D['P_kB']`: the distinct buffer sizes in kB of the P rows. The guard of line 376 allows one value only.
- The check number is the place of the check `P-rows` in the list, counted from 1. That check tests the fixed words that every P row shows the whole buffer on huge pages [Ref1].
- For part A the bullet says in fixed text that the page state was not recorded.
- The function `render` continues with section 1.5 at line 928. It ends at line 1488.
